slides.narration: Welcome to arrays and searching. In this part we learn what an array is, how to declare and fill it, and what happens when an index is wrong. We process arrays with loops, learn that an array name is a reference, and finish with linear search.

slides.heading: What is an array?
slides.body_md: An **array** stores many values of the **same data type** under one name. Each value is an **element** reached by its **index**, which starts at **0**. The property **length** gives the number of elements.

slides.heading: Declaring and creating an array
slides.body_md: The type is followed by **[ ]**. The operator **new** creates the array with its size. A list of values in braces creates and fills it at once.

visual.alt: Table of four ways to write an array: new with a size, brackets after the name, a list of values in curly brackets, and declaration and creation in separate statements
visual.caption: The size is given with new; a list of values fixes the length itself.

slides.narration: The type is followed by square brackets. The operator new creates the array in memory, with the size written in brackets. A list of values in curly brackets creates and fills the array in one statement, and Java counts the values itself. The brackets may come after the type or after the name, but after the type is the usual style.

slides.heading: Index and length
slides.body_md: Valid indexes are **0 to length - 1**. A wrong index compiles but stops the program with an **ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException**. **length** is a property: no brackets.

rows: run-time error: java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 5 out of bounds for length 5

slides.narration: Valid indexes run from zero to length minus one. An index outside this range compiles, but stops the program with an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, and the message names the index and the length. Length is a property, so it is written without brackets. With brackets, the compiler reports that it cannot find the symbol.

slides.heading: Searching: linear search
slides.body_md: **Searching** means finding the position of a value, the **key**, in an array. **Linear search** compares the key with each element in turn from the first, and needs **no particular order**.

nodes.label: Equal: note the position and stop

visual.alt: Flow of linear search: start at index 0, compare a[i] with the key, if equal note the position and stop, otherwise increase i, and if the end is passed the key is not found
visual.caption: Linear search checks the elements in turn.

slides.narration: Searching means finding where a value, called the key, is stored in an array. Linear search starts at the first element and compares each element with the key in turn. It stops when a match is found or when the array ends. It needs no particular order in the array.

slides.heading: Linear search with a found flag

visual.alt: Table of linear search in {14, 27, 9, 33, 21, 8}: key 33 gives Found at index 3 after 4 comparisons; key 8 needs 6 comparisons; key 50 is not found after 6 comparisons
visual.caption: The array is {14, 27, 9, 33, 21, 8}; pos starts at -1.

slides.narration: The position is kept in the variable pos, which starts at minus one. When an element equals the key, pos gets the index and break leaves the loop. After the loop, minus one means the key was not found. For the key thirty three the answer is index three, and for the key fifty the answer is not found.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: tracing the search
slides.body_md: Trace the search for the key **33** in the array {14, 27, 9, 33, 21, 8}.

visual.alt: Trace table of the search for 33: elements 14, 27 and 9 give false, element 33 at index 3 gives true, so pos becomes 3 and the loop stops after four comparisons
visual.caption: The last two elements are never examined.

slides.narration: Trace the search for thirty three. Element zero is fourteen, element one is twenty seven, and element two is nine, so all three comparisons fail. Element three is thirty three, so pos becomes three and the loop stops after four comparisons. The remaining two elements are never examined.

slides.heading: How much work does linear search do?
slides.body_md: The work depends on **where the key is**: one comparison at best, **n comparisons** at worst, when the key is last or absent.

visual.alt: Table of the work of linear search on six elements: key 14 needs 1, key 9 needs 3, key 8 needs 6, key 50 needs 6 comparisons
visual.caption: Best case: 1 comparison. Worst case: n comparisons.

slides.narration: The work depends on where the key is. If it is the first element, one comparison is enough. If it is the last element, or not in the array at all, every element is compared. For six elements that is one comparison at best and six at worst.

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: declaring an array, index and length, the exception for a bad index, processing with a loop, arrays as references and linear search

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. An array is created with new, its elements start with default values, and its indexes run from zero to length minus one. A wrong index stops the program at run time. Loops process arrays, and a maximum should start with the first element. An array name is a reference. Linear search compares in turn, with the position starting at minus one.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: `length` for an array has no brackets; `length()` belongs to a String.
Start a maximum or minimum with `a[0]`, not with `0`.
`b = a` does not copy an array: both names refer to the same array.
In a search program set the position to `-1` first, use `break` on a match, and test the flag after the loop.
slides.narration: Some exam tips. Write the loop condition with less than the length, never less than or equal. Length for an array has no brackets. Start a maximum or minimum with the first element. Remember that assigning one array name to another does not copy the elements. In a search program set the position to minus one first, use break on a match, and test the flag after the loop.

slides.narration: The outer loop makes n minus one passes, because the last element is then automatically in place. In each pass the inner loop finds the index of the smallest element, called min. slides.heading: Bubble sort: compare neighbours
slides.body_md: In **bubble sort** each pass compares **adjacent** elements and swaps a pair that is out of order. The largest element **bubbles** to the end.

slides.narration: In bubble sort, each pass compares adjacent elements and swaps a pair that is out of order. The table shows pass one on the same five numbers. Twenty nine is swapped with fourteen. Twenty nine and thirty seven are already in order. Then thirty seven is swapped with eight and with twenty two. The largest element has bubbled to the end.

rows: the last i elements are already in place; a[j + 1] must stay inside the array
a neighbouring pair that is out of order for ascending order

slides.narration: The outer loop counts the passes. The inner loop compares a pair of neighbours and swaps them if they are out of order. Its limit is n minus one minus i, because after i passes the last i elements are already in their final places, and because the program reads the element after j, which must stay inside the array.

slides.heading: Selection sort or bubble sort?
slides.body_md: Both need **n - 1** passes. **Selection sort** swaps once per pass; **bubble sort** may swap many times. Both are fine for the small arrays of ICSE programs.

On the array twenty nine, fourteen, thirty seven, eight, twenty two, selection sort swaps two times and bubble sort six times. On a reversed array of five values, selection sort swaps twice and bubble sort ten times.

slides.body_md: When roll numbers and marks are stored in **parallel arrays**, a swap in one array must be made in the other at the **same positions**.

If the marks are sorted, every swap must also be made in the roll number array, at the same positions. Otherwise the pairs would be broken. slides.narration: To sum up Part 2. Binary search needs a sorted array and halves the range at each step, using low, high and mid. It makes far fewer comparisons than linear search. Selection sort makes n minus one passes, swapping the smallest element into place. Bubble sort compares neighbours. Descending order reverses the comparison. Parallel arrays are swapped together.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Loop condition `i <= a.length` (index out of bounds), or `a.length()` with brackets.
- Starting a maximum with 0 when the values can be negative.
- Thinking `b = a` copies an array.
- Forgetting `break` in a search, or not testing the flag value `-1` after the loop.
- Using binary search on an unsorted array, or computing `mid` wrongly (use integer division).
- Wrong inner limit in bubble sort, or the swap inside the inner search loop of selection sort.
- Swapping only one of two parallel arrays.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Output questions: each line of the passes in the exact order.
- Trace questions: low, high and mid at every step.
- Programs (15 marks): class header and Scanner, array filled in a loop, the search or sort logic with correct limits, clear output, variable description.

questions.stem_md: What does selection sort (ascending order) do in each pass?

options.text_md: It compares neighbouring elements and swaps them whenever they are out of order

**Correct option: (a)** `Pass 1: 9 31 62 48 20`. In the first pass the smallest element, 9 at index 3, is found and swapped with the element at index 0, which gives `Pass 1: 9 31 62 48 20`. **Correct option: (d)** `4`. There are 5 passes. The last pass finds 12 already at index 4, so no swap is made there, and the counter shows `4`. Selection sort makes at most one swap per pass; bubble sort on the same data would make `8` swaps.

With a[j] < a[max] the same loop would pick the smallest element and display `Pass 1: 8 40 22 15 / Pass 2: 8 15 22 40 / Pass 3: 8 15 22 40`; the option a[max] > a[j] means the same as that one.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Selection sort** finds the smallest (or largest) element of the unsorted part in each pass and swaps it into place once, so it makes at most n - 1 swaps. **Bubble sort** compares neighbouring elements and swaps them whenever they are out of order, so the large values move gradually to the end and many swaps may be needed.

questions.stem_md: In bubble sort (ascending order), what is done to two adjacent elements a[j] and a[j + 1] during a pass?

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** They are compared and swapped if a[j] is greater than a[j + 1]. Bubble sort repeatedly passes over the array, compares each pair of neighbours and swaps a pair that is in the wrong order. After a pass the largest unsorted element has moved to the end, like a bubble rising.

**Correct option: (c)** `Pass 1: 18 40 7 26 53`. In pass 1 every adjacent pair is compared once: 53 is swapped past 18, 40, 7 and 26, so the largest value goes to the end and the line is `Pass 1: 18 40 7 26 53`. The other options are the first pass of selection sort, the second line of this program and the first pass of the descending version.

**Correct option: (d)** `6`. Each swap removes one pair that is out of order, and this array has 6 such pairs (3 is before 1 and 2, 8 is before 1, 6 and 2, and 6 is before 2), so 6 swaps are made. Selection sort needs only `2` on the same data, the number of comparisons is 10, and the number of passes is 4.

questions.stem_md: In bubble sort the inner loop is written as for (int j = 0; j < n - 1 - i; j++) in pass number i (counted from 0). Why is its limit n - 1 - i?

options.text_md: The first element never needs to be compared with anything
The array has only n - 1 elements
It makes the inner loop run exactly once in every pass
The last i elements are already in their final places, and a[j + 1] must stay inside the array

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The last i elements are already in their final places, and a[j + 1] must stay inside the array. Every pass carries the largest remaining value to the end, so the last i elements need no more comparisons, and because the loop reads a[j + 1] the largest allowed j is n - 2 even in the first pass. Writing j < n - i makes the first pass read a[n] and stops the program with `java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 4 out of bounds for length 4`.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** `if (a[j] < a[j + 1])`. For a descending order a pair is wrong when the left element is smaller than the right one, so the test is reversed to a[j] < a[j + 1]. On {24, 9, 31, 17} the last pass of that program gives `Pass 3: 31 24 17 9`. The test a[j] == a[j + 1] swaps only equal values, and a[j] < a[j - 1] fails at j = 0 with `java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index -1 out of bounds for length 4`.
